1. How was the content ratio of HCA, Mn2+, Mn-hCaO2, hZIF8 NPs, and SMA screened and
determined? The authors did not mention the basis for screening.
Response: We apologize for lack of clarity in the original manuscript and have included this
rationalization. The selection of each component was guided by specific functional and
structural considerations. The ratio of HCA was adopted based on our previous work
optimizing polyphenol-based functionalization of hydrogels11. The concentration of Mn²⁺ was
tuned to maximize the oxygen-release performance of the composite. We found that
supplementing 3 mg of MnCl₂ per 5 g of CaCl₂ precursor resulted in optimal oxygen generation
kinetics. Higher Mn²⁺ levels led to a rapid burst release of oxygen with short duration, whereas
lower amounts yielded insufficient catalytic activity. The SMA concentration of 15% was
chosen in accordance with established protocols from prior literature12. The relative proportion
of hZIF-8 and Mn-hCaO₂ was optimized through mechanical testing. Excessive Mn-hCaO₂
impeded the photo-crosslinking process due to light absorption by the dark-colored particles.
Meanwhile, incorporation of hZIF-8 improved compressive strength through
nanoreinforcement, although excess amounts adversely affected hydrogel integrity. Thus, the
present hydrogel formulation was systematically optimized and rationally designed.

6. During the rat periodontitis model construction, the hydrogels were irradiated by blue-violet

Response: We thank the reviewer for raising these important methodological points. Regarding
light exposure, 395 nm blue-violet light has been established as safe in multiple biomedical
contexts. To directly assess biocompatibility, we exposed human periodontal ligament stem
cells (hPDLSCs) to 30 seconds of irradiation and evaluated viability via CCK-8 assay over 48

Concerning treatment frequency, a single application was chosen to align with principles of
minimal intervention. Repeated injections into periodontal pockets could impede natural
healing processes due to physical obstruction and increase patient discomfort, thereby
compromising clinical feasibility. The sustained bioactive effects of the hydrogel over four
weeks further support the rationale for a single-dose regimen.

periodontal pocket. Isn’t the periodontal pocket area more rational? It is doubted that the

Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this pertinent point regarding the site selection
for histological analysis. The periodontal pocket represents the direct application site of the
hydrogel and more closely mimics horizontal bone loss commonly observed in human
periodontitis. However, the choice of the root furcation area in this rat model was based on
experimental considerations. The anatomy of the rat first molar, which usually has 4-5 roots,
introduces notable variability in interdental bone structure, which may compromise the
reproducibility of quantitative assessments. In the contrast, the furcation region exhibits
consistent and pronounced susceptibility to inflammatory bone resorption in rat periodontitis
model, and its well-defined anatomical boundaries allow for reliable and comparable
histological measurements. Therefore, the root furcation region was widely employed in
periodontitis studies using SD rats. To provide a comprehensive perspective, we have now
supplemented the revised manuscript with H&E staining images of the periodontal pocket area,
including gingival and interdental bone tissues.

Experimental sections
Line 954-965
“In vitro Antibacterial Assay
Porphyromonas gingivalis (ATCC 33277) was routinely cultured under anaerobic conditions
(85% N₂, 10% H₂, 5% CO₂) at 37°C in brain heart infusion (BHI) broth supplemented with 5
mg L-1 hemin and 1 mg L-1 vitamin K. The bacteria were suspended with a density 1×108 CFU
mL−1 and co-cultured with different groups of respective hydrogels (1mm height, diameter in
line with the 24-well plate). After 24 hours of anaerobic incubation, the bacteria were harvested
by centrifugation at 6000 g for 10 min and washed twice with PBS. Bacterial viability was
confirmed by colony-forming unit (CFU) measured with optical density at 600 nm. For SEM
imaging, bacterial pellets were fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde over night at 4°C. Samples were
then dehydrated through a graded ethanol series (30%, 50%, 70%, 90%, and 100%, 10 min
each). Then they were mounted on silicon wafers, sputter-coated with gold, and observed under
a scanning electron microscope.”
